title: Lesson 5 - A1.2.4 Social Engineering
subject: Information Technology

sections.heading: What is social engineering?
sections.text: Social engineering is when attackers trick people into giving away secure information. It relies on deception rather than technical hacking: it manipulates people's desire to do the right thing.
points: The aim: engage the target, gain their trust, and extract key information
Example: a fake email pretending to be your bank asks you to 'verify your password'
Example: a scam phone call claims to be from IT support and asks for login details
Humans are usually the weakest link in any security, so training staff is essential
Defence: spot fake emails, messages and calls before responding; don't click suspicious links or share personal information

head: Attack
How it reaches you
Example
rows: A fake email from 'your bank' with a link to a site that installs malware or harvests usernames and passwords
A caller pretending to be IT support or your bank asks for login details
'Your parcel has been redirected due to an unpaid shipping fee. Visit postoffice-redelivery…'

sections.heading: Phishing: the most common attack
points: Tools on the dark web copy emails and websites from real organisations
The emails look legitimate and contain links to sites that carry malware or harvest usernames and passwords
Tells: a sense of urgency, not personalised (e.g. 'Hi there'), a link that seems 'off'
Phishing tools are getting more sophisticated, so they're hard to spot when you're in a hurry

sections.heading: Smishing tells: real examples from the slides
sections.text: Every one of these texts on your slides is fake. Look for the same warning signs:
points: Urgency or threats: 'formal warning and £250 fine', 'arrest warrant', 'to avoid fees'
Look-alike links that aren't the real site: authorisedevice365.com, ee.uk.billing45.com, gov.uk-repay.com, postoffice-redelivery
Unexpected good news: a tax rebate or a 'loyalty reward' on a parcel you didn't order
Asking you to pay, update billing details, or follow a link to 'secure' your account
Pretending to be trusted names: GOV.UK, EE, Amazon, Post Office, the tax office

sections.heading: Phishing vs spear phishing vs whaling

head: Type
Who it targets
Slide example
rows: Mass mailing to lots of people
'Hi there, It is time to reset your account so your phone will update. Click here'
A carefully chosen target, with personalised language, tone and wording
'Jack, please confirm your details… so we can send you a substantial discount on your bill for your loyalty'
Spear phishing aimed at high net-worth, powerful people (e.g. a CEO)
'Dear Grace, As CEO we need you to confirm your company's entitlement to a discount on your corporate account'

sections.heading: Pretexting and impersonation
sections.text: Pretexting is creating a deceptive scenario to get access to information, systems or services. The attacker invents a fake situation and poses as a trusted person who can sort it out.
points: Most pretexts have two parts: a character (who they pretend to be) and a situation (the made-up problem)
It makes a later social engineering attack more likely to succeed
Protect yourself: check credentials and verify who you're speaking to
Ask for a direct line to call back, and check the number against your bank card, statements or other official materials

sections.heading: What is DNS?
sections.text: The Domain Name System (DNS) turns domain names (like google.com) into IP addresses, which browsers use to load web pages. Every internet-connected device has its own IP address so other devices can find it.
points: 1. Your device sends a DNS query: 'What is the IP address of www.google.com?'
2. The DNS server replies with the IP address
3. Your device sends the web request to that IP address

sections.heading: DNS spoofing
sections.text: The hacker inserts a fraudulent DNS entry. When the user asks for the genuine website, the request resolves to a malicious look-alike site instead.
points: The fake site looks like the official one, so it's a perfect phishing trap
It can collect passwords, banking information, card numbers, contact details and location data
Users rarely notice the small red flags on a spoofed site
Big red flag: the fake site usually has no encryption certificate, so the connection is unencrypted (cleartext)
Browsers warn when a connection isn't secure, but many people ignore it and log in anyway

diagram.alt: Left: a normal DNS lookup. You ask the DNS server for the IP address of bank.com, it replies with the real IP, and you reach the real bank site. Right: DNS spoofing. A hacker inserts a fake entry into the DNS server, so when you ask for bank.com it replies with a fake IP and you land on a fake look-alike site that steals your login details; the real site is never reached. A red flag is the missing padlock or a 'Not secure' warning.
diagram.caption: A poisoned DNS entry sends you to a fake look-alike site instead of the real one.

sections.heading: Tools to identify a host or IP address
points: Reverse DNS lookup: turn an IP address into a host name (e.g. dnschecker.org reverse DNS)
DNS record lookup: find all the DNS records and IP addresses for a host name or URL
Useful when checking firewall logs or intrusion detection tools: an unrecognised source can be added to the firewall's deny list
Useful for blocking staff from untrusted websites or subdomains

keyIdea: Social engineering attacks people, not computers. Attackers use deception (fake emails, calls, texts, made-up scenarios and spoofed websites) to win trust and steal information, so spotting the tells, verifying who you're dealing with, and training staff are the key defences.
flashcards: Social engineering
Tricking people into giving away secure information. It relies on deception, not technical hacking.
Phishing
Fake emails that look legitimate, with links to malware or sites that harvest usernames and passwords.
Vishing
Voice phishing: scam phone calls or voice messages, e.g. fake IT support asking for login details.
Smishing
SMS phishing: scam text messages, e.g. a fake parcel redelivery fee with a link.
Spear phishing
A targeted phishing attack on a carefully chosen person, with personalised language and wording.
Whaling
Spear phishing aimed at high net-worth, powerful people such as a CEO.
Phishing tells
A sense of urgency, not personalised, a link that seems 'off'.
Look-alike link
A web address made to look real but isn't, e.g. gov.uk-repay.com or ee.uk.billing45.com.
Pretexting
Creating a deceptive scenario to get information, posing as a trusted person who can solve a fake problem.
Two parts of a pretext
A character (who they pretend to be) and a situation (the made-up problem).
Impersonation
Pretending to be someone trustworthy, like a bank, IT support or a manager.
Defending against pretexting
Check credentials, verify identity, and call back on a number from your card or statement.
Weakest link
Humans are usually the weakest link in security, which is why staff training is essential.
DNS
Domain Name System: turns domain names into IP addresses so browsers can load pages.
IP address
A unique number for every internet-connected device, used by other devices to find it.
DNS query
A request asking a DNS server for the IP address of a domain name.
DNS spoofing
A hacker inserts a fraudulent DNS entry, so requests for a real site go to a fake look-alike site.
Spoofed website
A fake site that looks like the official one, used to steal passwords, bank and card details.
Encryption certificate red flag
Spoofed sites usually have no certificate, so the connection is unencrypted (cleartext) and the browser warns you.
Cleartext
Data sent without encryption, so it can be read if intercepted.
Reverse DNS lookup
A tool that turns an IP address back into a host name.
Firewall deny list
A list of blocked sources. Unrecognised IPs found in logs can be added to it.

o: Tricking people into giving away secure information
quiz.e: It relies on deception: manipulating people rather than hacking technology.

quiz.q: What is the difference between phishing, vishing and smishing?
o: Phishing = phone, vishing = video, smishing = social media
Phishing = email, vishing = voice calls, smishing = text messages
quiz.e: Same trick, different channel: email, voice (phone) or SMS (text).

o: A phishing email sent to millions of people
A targeted, personalised phishing attack on a chosen person
Fishing for passwords on the dark web
quiz.e: Spear phishing picks its target carefully and personalises the message.

o: Sending a text message before a call
Creating a fake scenario and posing as a trusted person to get information
quiz.e: A pretext is a made-up situation plus a fake character who can 'solve' it.

o: Users are sent to a fake site that looks real, and enter their details
quiz.e: Because the fake site looks official, people hand over passwords, bank and card details.

quiz.q: Which is the most common type of social engineering attack?
quiz.e: Your slides say phishing is the most common.

quiz.q: An email says 'Dear Grace, As CEO we need you to confirm your company's entitlement…'. Which attack is this?
quiz.e: It targets a powerful, senior person (a CEO), so it's whaling.

quiz.q: Which of these is a phishing 'tell'?
o: It uses your full name and account number correctly
It creates a sense of urgency and has a link that seems 'off'
It comes from someone you're expecting
It has no links at all
quiz.e: Urgency, a generic greeting and odd-looking links are classic tells.

quiz.q: A text says your EE bill couldn't be processed and links to ee.uk.billing45.com. What's the main warning sign?
o: The link is a look-alike address, not EE's real site
It was sent in the afternoon
It's a text, not an email
quiz.e: The domain is billing45.com dressed up to look like EE. That's smishing.

quiz.q: What are the two main parts of most pretexts?
o: An IP address and a domain
quiz.e: The attacker plays a character and invents a situation for you.

quiz.q: Someone calls claiming to be your bank. What's the safest thing to do?
o: Give them your PIN to prove who you are
Ask them to text you instead
Hang up and call back on the number on your bank card
quiz.e: Verify identity by calling back on an official number from your card or statement.

o: Turns domain names into IP addresses
quiz.e: Browsers need the IP address, and DNS looks it up from the domain name.

quiz.q: In DNS spoofing, what does the hacker change?
o: A DNS entry, so the real domain points to a fake site
quiz.e: A fraudulent DNS entry makes requests for the real site resolve to the malicious one.

quiz.q: What red flag often appears on a spoofed website?
o: It asks you to log in
No encryption certificate, so the browser warns the connection isn't secure
quiz.e: Spoofed sites usually use an unencrypted (cleartext) connection, and browsers warn about it.

quiz.q: Why are humans called 'the weakest link' in security?
o: Attackers can trick them, even when the technology is secure
quiz.e: Social engineering targets people's trust and wish to help, which is why staff training matters.

quiz.q: An IT technician finds an unknown IP address in the firewall logs. What can a reverse DNS lookup do?
o: Turn the IP address into a host name to identify the source
quiz.e: Once identified, an untrusted source can be added to the firewall's deny list.

apply.title: Name that scam
apply.intro: Read each message or situation and pick the attack, or the best response. Several come straight from your slides.

items.task: Text: 'A new device has successfully logged in at 19:25. If this was not authorised by you follow this link: www.authorisedevice365.com'
items.e: A scam text with a look-alike link is smishing (SMS phishing).

items.task: A phone call: 'Hi, it's IT support. We've spotted a problem with your account, can you read me your password so I can fix it?'
items.e: Voice phishing by phone, using a pretext (a fake IT problem).

items.task: An email to thousands of people: 'Hi there, It is time to reset your account so your phone will update. Click here to reset'
items.e: A mass, non-personalised email is standard phishing.

items.task: Email: 'Jack, please confirm your details by clicking the link below so we can send you a substantial discount on your bill for your loyalty.'
items.e: It's personalised to one chosen person: spear phishing.

items.task: Text: 'GOV.UK ALERT: You have been out of the house more than once. We are issuing you a £250 fine… Call 0800 345 9999.'
items.e: Threats, fines and urgency in a text are classic smishing tells.

items.task: You type your bank's correct web address, but end up on a fake copy of the site. The browser warns the connection isn't secure.
items.e: A fraudulent DNS entry sent you to a look-alike site. The missing encryption is the red flag.

items.task: A caller says they're from the bank's fraud team and need to 'verify' your card number. What should you do?
o: Hang up and call the number on the back of your card
items.e: Verify the person by calling back on an official number. Never use one they give you.

items.task: Someone dressed as a delivery driver says they need to 'just pop in' to the server room to collect a parcel.
items.e: A fake character plus a fake situation: a pretext to gain access.

items.task: Text: 'Post Office: Your parcel has been redirected due to an unpaid shipping fee. To reschedule a delivery please visit postoffice-redelivery…'
items.e: An unexpected fee, urgency and a look-alike link are smishing tells.

items.task: A company's finance director gets a carefully written email, addressed to her by name and job title, asking her to approve a large transfer.
items.e: A personalised attack on a senior, powerful person is whaling.

items.task: Text: 'Records show that you have a pending tax rebate. To calculate your claim, click here: gov.uk-repay.com'
items.e: Unexpected good news plus a fake 'gov.uk' address is smishing.

items.task: The IT team finds an unknown IP address repeatedly trying to connect in the firewall logs. What should they do?
o: Use a reverse DNS lookup to identify it, then add it to the firewall's deny list
items.e: Identify the source, and if it's untrusted, block it on the firewall.

pts: Tricking or manipulating people into giving away secure information
using deception rather than technical hacking
exam.tip: Two parts: what happens (people are tricked) and how (deception, not technical hacking).

exam.q: 2. Describe the difference between phishing, vishing and smishing.
pts: Phishing uses fake emails
Vishing uses phone calls or voice messages
Smishing uses text (SMS) messages
exam.tip: One mark each: name the channel for each attack.

pts: A targeted phishing attack on a carefully chosen person
using personalised language, tone and wording
exam.tip: Contrast it with normal phishing (mass mailing) to show understanding.

exam.q: 4. Explain the difference between spear phishing and whaling.
pts: Spear phishing targets a chosen individual with a personalised message
whereas whaling is spear phishing aimed specifically at high net-worth or powerful people, e.g. a CEO
exam.tip: Whaling is a type of spear phishing, so say what makes it special: the target.

exam.q: 5. What is pretexting in social engineering?
pts: Creating a deceptive scenario (a fake situation)
and posing as a trusted person (a character) who can resolve it, to get information or access
exam.tip: Mention both parts of a pretext: the character and the situation.

exam.q: 6. Describe how a DNS spoofing attack works.
pts: The hacker inserts a fraudulent DNS entry
The user requests the genuine website
The request resolves to the IP address of a fake look-alike website instead
exam.tip: Follow the diagram on the slides: hacker → user's request → fake site.

exam.q: 7. Explain why DNS spoofing is dangerous.
pts: The fake website looks like the official one, with no obvious red flags
so users trust it and enter passwords, bank or card details
Many users miss or ignore the browser's warning that the connection isn't encrypted
exam.tip: Why it works (it looks real) + what's stolen + why people don't notice.

exam.sc: Oakwood Estate Agents has 25 staff and stores clients' bank details for deposits. The managing director, Sarah Khan, regularly posts about the business on social media. Staff often get phone calls from people saying they are from 'IT support', and they use their work phones for texts from clients. Staff have never had any security training.
exam.q: 8. Sarah Khan receives an email addressed to her by name, mentioning her role as managing director and a recent social media post. Identify the type of attack.
pts: Whaling (accept: spear phishing aimed at a senior person)

exam.sc: Oakwood Estate Agents has 25 staff and stores clients' bank details for deposits. The managing director, Sarah Khan, regularly posts about the business on social media. Staff often get phone calls from people saying they are from 'IT support', and they use their work phones for texts from clients. Staff have never had any security training.
exam.q: 9. Explain two ways Oakwood Estate Agents could protect its staff from vishing and pretexting calls.
pts: Way 1, e.g. train staff to recognise social engineering techniques
so they know never to give passwords to callers claiming to be IT support
Way 2, e.g. a policy to verify callers by calling back on a known, official number
so an impersonator can't prove a fake identity and the attack fails
exam.tip: Link each method to the scenario: the 'IT support' calls and the lack of training.

exam.sc: Oakwood Estate Agents has 25 staff and stores clients' bank details for deposits. The managing director, Sarah Khan, regularly posts about the business on social media. Staff often get phone calls from people saying they are from 'IT support', and they use their work phones for texts from clients. Staff have never had any security training.
exam.q: 10. Evaluate whether staff training would be enough to protect Oakwood Estate Agents from social engineering attacks.
pts: Strength: humans are the weakest link, and staff have had no training, so training tackles the main weakness
Strength: trained staff can spot tells (urgency, look-alike links, odd callers) in emails, calls and texts
Weakness: phishing tools are increasingly sophisticated and hard to spot in a hurry, so trained staff can still be fooled
Weakness: some attacks, like DNS spoofing, send users to convincing fake sites without them doing anything obviously wrong
Other measures: verify-and-call-back procedures, reviewing what Sarah posts publicly, firewall deny lists and blocking untrusted sites
Justified conclusion: training is the most important defence but not enough on its own; it should be combined with policies and technical controls
exam.tip: Top-grade "evaluate" = strengths AND weaknesses, linked to Oakwood, then a clear judgement with a reason.
